title: The Keeper's Daughter
text: Nell had lived in the lighthouse for eleven years, and in all that time she had never once slept through a storm. Her father said this was because she had been born during one, as though the weather had marked her as its own on the very first night of her life.

Tonight the wind came in long, shuddering pushes that made the iron staircase hum. Nell counted the gaps between them the way other children counted sheep. Her father was above her in the lamp room, and she could hear the slow scrape of his boots as he walked his circle around the great glass eye of the light.

At half past two the scraping stopped. Nell sat up. She waited for it to begin again, and when it did not, she was already halfway up the stairs before she had decided to move at all. Her candle went out on the third turn, but she did not need it. She knew the number of steps better than she knew her own age.
She found him at the top, kneeling beside the mechanism with his sleeves pushed back, and the relief that flooded through her was so sudden that it came out as anger. 'You stopped walking,' she said.
'The gear's slipping,' he answered, without looking up. 'Fetch the small oil can, Nell. Quickly now.' And because there was a ship somewhere out in all that black water, she went.

title: Saturday at the Market
text: Otis did not like Saturdays, and he liked market days least of all. It was not the crowds, exactly, nor the smell of frying onions that clung to his jumper for days afterwards. It was that his grandmother expected him to be useful, and being useful meant standing behind the vegetable stall shouting prices at strangers.
'Louder,' she said, without turning round. 'A voice like that will lose us the day.'
Otis tried again. The words came out thin and apologetic, and a woman inspecting the parsnips looked up, smiled kindly, and put them back down.

His grandmother sighed the particular sigh she kept for him. Then she did something unexpected: she came and stood beside him, put one hand flat on the trestle table, and said nothing at all for a full minute. When the next customer approached, she waited. Otis, unable to bear the silence, spoke first — and this time his voice carried right across the square.
'There,' said his grandmother, moving away again. 'You had it all along. You were simply waiting for me to do it for you.'

title: The Causeway
text: The island could be reached on foot for four hours either side of low tide, and Isaac had checked the times twice before setting out. He had written them on the back of his hand in biro: 11:20, and then, underlined, 15:20. Four hours. It had seemed an enormous amount of time when he was standing on the mainland with the whole afternoon ahead of him.

It seemed a good deal less enormous now. The causeway behind him had begun to shine in a way it had not shone an hour ago, and the shine was spreading, the way spilt water spreads across a table — slowly, and then all at once.
He told himself there was no need to hurry. He told himself this several times, quite firmly, and then he began to run.

The water reached the causeway before he did. It came from both sides at once, which was the part nobody had warned him about; he had imagined it creeping in politely from one direction, giving him a chance to outpace it. Instead it simply arrived, cold and unhurried, and closed over the stones as though they had never been there.

There was a wooden refuge box on stilts halfway along, put there for people exactly as foolish as he had been. Isaac climbed the ladder, sat down on the damp bench inside, and watched the last of the path disappear. He was not in any danger. He was, however, going to have to explain this, and that was almost worse.

title: The New Girl
text: For the first three days, nobody could pronounce her name properly, and Marguerite let them all get it wrong. She said nothing at registration when Mr Okafor said 'Margaret'. She said nothing in the dinner queue when a boy with a football under his arm called her 'Margarine' and looked round to see who was laughing.
Her mother asked, on the third evening, how school was going. 'Fine,' said Marguerite, which was true in the way that a photograph of a room is true.

On the fourth day something small happened. A girl called Priya, who had not laughed at the football boy's joke and had not defended her either, leaned across during silent reading and said, quite quietly, 'How do you actually say it?'
Marguerite told her. Priya repeated it, got it slightly wrong, frowned, and tried again. She got it right the second time and then said it a third time, as though filing it away somewhere safe.

It was not a friendship yet. It was not even a conversation, really. But Marguerite found that she was looking forward to silent reading the next day, and that was more than she had felt about anything since the move.

title: The Sunflower Contest
text: The rule of the contest was simple, and Grandad had explained it in October when the seeds went in: whoever grew the tallest sunflower by the last Saturday in August would not have to wash up for a month. Priya had taken this extremely seriously. She had measured hers every Sunday and written the numbers in a notebook with a ruled column for the date, as though a plant could be persuaded by good record-keeping.

Grandad had not measured his once. He watered it when he happened to be passing, spoke to it occasionally in a low voice she could never quite catch, and otherwise appeared to forget it existed. By July his sunflower was a head taller than hers, and Priya had begun to find the whole thing personally insulting.

"It's the wall," he said, when she finally asked. "Mine's against the brick. Holds the heat overnight. Yours is out in the open getting a lovely view and no supper." He said it without any triumph at all, which somehow made it worse.

On the last Saturday in August, Priya's sunflower was two metres and four centimetres, and Grandad's was two metres and nineteen. She wrote both numbers in her notebook, because a record was a record, and then she stood looking at the wall for a long while.

The following October, when the new seeds went in, Grandad found that every one of his had somehow been planted in the middle of the lawn, and that the whole length of the warm brick wall had been left, quite deliberately, for somebody else. He laughed for a good minute. Then he went and fetched a second notebook, and asked her whether she would like a ruled column for the weather as well.

title: Mooring at Dusk
text: The boat was called the Marigold, which Ben thought was a ridiculous name for something painted that particular shade of green, and it moved at exactly the speed of a person walking without hurrying. This had annoyed him for the first two days. By the fourth he had stopped noticing, and by the sixth he had begun to find anything faster slightly rude.

His aunt steered from the back with one hand and drank tea with the other, and never appeared to look where she was going. Ben had asked her about this. She said that on a canal there was nowhere else to go, so looking was mostly a formality, and that the useful thing was listening: to the engine, to the water at the bow, to the particular hollow note the hull made when the channel shallowed.

They moored that evening below a lock, in the last of the light, where the hedges came right down to the towpath. Ben hammered in the mooring pins himself. He got the first one crooked and the second one right, and his aunt said nothing about either, which he appreciated more than praise.

After supper the engine was off and the difference was extraordinary. Sounds he had not known were there arrived one after another: a moorhen somewhere in the reeds, a car on a road he could not see, the water moving against the hull in small irregular slaps, and, further off, the wind going through a field of something tall.

He had told his friends that a week on a canal boat sounded like a week of nothing happening. Sitting on the roof with a blanket round him, watching the last of the colour go out of the sky behind the lock gates, he found he could not think of a way to explain that he had been wrong without sounding like somebody much older than eleven.

title: The Birds That Almost Never Land
text: Of all the birds that visit Britain each summer, the swift is the one most people have seen without ever knowing what they were looking at. It is a dark, scythe-shaped bird, screaming in parties around rooftops on warm evenings in June. It is often mistaken for a swallow or a house martin, and it is neither.

What makes the swift remarkable is not its speed, though it is fast, but the sheer amount of its life spent in the air. A young swift leaving its nest in a British roof may not touch down again for two or even three years. In that time it will feed, drink, gather nesting material and sleep entirely on the wing, and it will fly to Africa and back several times before it ever perches on anything.

Sleeping in flight sounds impossible, and for a long time nobody quite believed it. The evidence came from pilots, who reported seeing swifts at extraordinary heights at night, and later from tiny tracking devices light enough to be carried without harming the bird. Swifts climb to around two thousand metres at dusk, and are thought to rest one half of the brain at a time while continuing to fly.

Their numbers in Britain have fallen sharply, by more than half since the middle of the 1990s. The reason is unusually simple for a conservation problem: swifts nest in small gaps under the eaves of older buildings, and modern roof repairs seal those gaps up. A bird that returns each May to the exact same crevice may find, one year, that there is no longer a crevice there.

This also makes the problem unusually easy to help with. A swift box fixed high on a wall, or a special brick built into a new house, costs very little and lasts for decades. It is not often that saving a species is a matter of leaving a hole in a wall — but for the swift, very largely, it is.

title: Why the Local Library Still Matters
text: Whenever a council announces that it is closing a library, somebody will say that libraries have had their day. Everything is online now, the argument runs; a building full of paper books is a pleasant memory rather than a public necessity. The argument sounds modern and sensible. It is also, on inspection, mostly wrong.

Consider first who actually uses a library. It is not, in the main, people choosing between a borrowed novel and a bought one. It is a child doing homework in a warm room because the house is crowded; a jobseeker who needs a computer and an hour of quiet to fill in a form; a new parent at a rhyme-time session, talking to another adult for the first time that week. None of these needs is met by a website.

Supporters of closure often point to the cost. Yet the sums involved are strikingly small — a typical library service costs a household a few pounds a year, less than a single paperback. Set against that is the cost of what replaces it, which is usually nothing, and which falls hardest on the households least able to make up the difference themselves.

It is fair to say that libraries must change, and the best of them have. They now lend tools, run coding clubs, host warm spaces in winter and offer free access to newspapers and research databases that would cost an individual hundreds of pounds. A library that stood still would indeed deserve the accusation of being a museum. Very few have stood still.

The real question is not whether we can afford libraries but what kind of place we want a town to be. A library is one of the last buildings a person can enter, stay in for several hours, and leave again without being expected to spend a penny. Once such a place is gone, it is almost never rebuilt.
